1030.title: The teachers, closed
1030.hook: from Nagarjuna to the village grandmother
1030.howItsDone: Buddhists honor their teachers in chants of lineage, in portraits on altars and in memorial days, while the texts point to the teaching itself as the teacher after the Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Assaji walked his alms round and Sariputta followed him because of how he moved. Your line: by example. Did anyone catch your one small thing? Day one thousand thirty.

Lay them out like photographs on a long table. Nagarjuna, arguing that nothing stands on its own. Asanga, bending over a wounded dog. Shantideva, the monk the others thought was lazy, standing up to recite. Atisha keeping his bad-tempered cook. Milarepa hauling stones for towers he was told to tear down. Machig Labdron offering her body to fear. Dogen just sitting. Hakuin saying is that so. Ryokan wishing he could give a thief the moon. The nun Chiyono and her broken bucket. Ajahn Chah in the forest, Dipa Ma in her small apartment, Maha Ghosananda walking for peace. And at the end of the table, a photo with no name on it. A grandmother. Today closes the teachers.

Here's what's strange about this long run of teachers. The Buddha himself seemed to see it coming, and to warn against leaning on any one of them too hard. In the discourse on his final passing, Ananda is worried about what happens when the Buddha is gone. The answer, in T. W. Rhys Davids' translation, is this: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." Just before that, he tells Ananda he has no closed fist of a teacher, nothing kept back for a chosen few. And near the very end, as this path heard a few days ago, he says the teaching and the discipline will be their teacher after he is gone. So in the Buddha's own words, the real teacher is the teaching. Every name on that table is someone who carried it for a stretch and handed it on. That changes how the stories sound. Nagarjuna's logic and the grandmother's lamp-lighting are not competing. They're two people holding the same lamp at different points on the road. Some were brilliant, some were wild, some were quiet. Some were saints in their tradition's eyes, and this block also made room for teachers who failed. None of them is the point. The lamp is the point. The Pali word for a teacher is acariya. In this light, a good acariya is someone who points past themselves, toward the teaching. That's why the block ends where it does, with unknown teachers, with your own, with the listener becoming one. The line runs right up to the present: whoever practices today is somewhere on that table, holding the lamp for a while.

Here's the practice, if you'd like it: sit with one teacher's memory. Settle into the sitting, and let the breath find its own pace. Then choose one face from the table, a famous name or your grandmother or the stranger who once told you the truth. Don't review their whole life. Pick one moment: a dog, a bucket, a cup of tea, a word. Let that moment sit beside you while you breathe. If your mind wanders off, come back to the moment, the way you'd come back to a friend's voice in a noisy room. The bell holds the time.
The teachers. From Nagarjuna to the grandmother with no name, people who carried the teaching for a stretch, while, in the Buddha's words, the teaching itself stayed the teacher. Today's words.
Your line: they carried it. Today, when you pass something good along, a skill, a kindness, a story, notice that you're carrying it for a stretch too. Day one thousand thirty.

1031.title: Why tell hard history
1031.hook: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure
1031.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics recite the Vinaya, which records the incidents behind its rules, including quarrels and misconduct, and Buddhist teachers and historians also discuss the community's failures openly alongside its achievements.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the teachers, from Nagarjuna to the grandmother with no name. Your line: they carried it. What did you carry along for a stretch? Day one thousand thirty-one.

In the town of Kosambi, the monks are fighting. It started small, over whether one monk had broken a rule or not. Now the community has split in two. They argue in the meeting hall. They argue in the village. The Buddha himself comes and asks them to stop, and, the texts say, they tell him, more or less, to leave it to them. This is the Buddha's own community, during his own lifetime, and it's in the scriptures, kept and recited by the very tradition it embarrasses. Today opens a new stretch of the path: history held honestly. It starts with a question. Why tell the hard parts at all?

The quarrel at Kosambi is told in the Vinaya and in the Majjhima Nikaya, and it doesn't end with a miracle. The Buddha tries to reconcile them. Then he leaves. He walks off alone into the forest, and the texts describe him visiting a few monks who are living together in harmony, as if to see what a good community looks like. Then something ordinary happens back in Kosambi. The lay followers, the people who feed the monks, decide that monks who won't make peace don't get their respect or their alms. Hungry and embarrassed, the monks go and make it up. The Dhammapada has a verse that tradition links to this quarrel. In Max Muller's translation: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." So here's an answer to today's question. The tradition tells hard history because its own texts do. The sangha, the community, is made of people. People argue, get proud, misuse power, and also repair, apologize and endure. A story where the community never fails would be hard to believe, and harder to learn from. Over the next days this path will look at kings who protected monks and kings who used them, at persecutions, at monks who spoke for war and monks who marched for peace. None of it is told to score a point against Buddhists, and none of it is the whole picture. It's told the way Kosambi is told: plainly, with the failure and the repair side by side.

Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: hold a hard story gently. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a hard story from a group you belong to: a family, a team, a school, a faith, a country. Not the worst one. A medium one. Don't argue with it and don't defend anyone. Just let it be true. Notice where it lands in the body: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Breathe into that place. Then, if you can, find one person in that story who tried to repair something. Hold both. The bell holds the time.
Why tell hard history. Because the community is made of people who fail and repair, and because the texts themselves tell it, as at Kosambi. Today's words.
Your line: made of people. Today, when a group you love lets you down, try saying it once: made of people. Then look for whoever is trying to repair it. Day one thousand thirty-one.

1032.title: Kings and monks
1032.hook: rulers have protected the sangha and used it; both are true
1032.howItsDone: In some Buddhist countries today, governments still recognize, fund or regulate the sangha, and Buddhists debate how close monks should stand to political power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monks of Kosambi quarreled, the Buddha walked into the forest, and the lay followers brought them to their senses. Your line: made of people. Where did you see a group repair itself? Day one thousand thirty-two.

A king wants a war. King Ajatasattu of Magadha has decided to attack his neighbors, the Vajjians, and before he does, he sends his chief minister to the Buddha. Tell him I'm going to attack, the king says. Then come back and report exactly what he says. It's a strange errand: a ruler using a holy man as a source of intelligence. The Buddha doesn't answer the minister directly. He turns to Ananda, who is fanning him, and starts asking questions about how the Vajjians live. That's how the discourse on the Buddha's final passing opens: with a king, a war plan, and a teacher who won't simply be used.

The Buddha's questions are about the Vajjians' habits. Do they meet often, and in harmony? Do they honor their elders? Do they protect their shrines and the holy people living among them? As long as they do, he says, they can be expected to prosper, not decline. The minister draws his own conclusion and leaves. Then the Buddha gathers his monks and gives them a matching list for the sangha. The point is quiet but sharp: a community's strength is in how it lives, not in who is fighting on its side. That opening is a good lens for the long history of kings and monks, because rulers have done both things to the sangha. They have protected it, and they have used it. The emperor Ashoka is one well-known case. His own inscriptions, carved in stone, express remorse over his conquest of Kalinga and speak of a new aim, conquest by dhamma. He supported monks and sent out envoys. Tradition, especially in Sri Lanka's chronicles, also says royal power was used to expel monks the court judged false. Protection and control arrived in the same hand. Across Asia, the pattern repeats in different forms. Kings built monasteries and appointed heads of the order. They also leaned on the robe to make their rule look blessed. The Pali texts have a word for the ideal: dhammaraja, a king who rules by dhamma. History holds rulers who reached for that ideal and rulers who borrowed the title. Both are true at once, and the tradition's own texts keep the question open.

Here's the practice, if you'd like it: notice one use of power. Settle the body and breathe for a few rounds. Then think about the last day or two. Find one moment when someone used power: a boss, a parent, a government, a platform, you. Don't judge it yet. Just ask the Buddha's kind of question. Did it protect someone? Did it use someone? Could it have done both? Stay with the picture, breathing, until you can see both sides of it without rushing to a verdict. The bell holds the time.
Kings and monks. Rulers have protected the sangha and used it, sometimes in the same breath, from Ajatasattu's errand to Ashoka's edicts and beyond. Today's words.
Your line: protected and used. Today, when someone powerful offers you support, a promotion, a platform, a favor, ask quietly what comes attached. Day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: Persecutions
1033.hook: monasteries closed in Tang China and temples torn down in Japan when Buddhism was split from the state
1033.howItsDone: Buddhist communities in China and Japan remember these persecutions in their histories, and temples that were closed or destroyed have in places been rebuilt and are active today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kings and monks: Ajatasattu's errand, Ashoka's remorse, the sangha held close by power. Your line was protected and used. What came attached to the support you were offered? Day one thousand thirty-three.

A bronze Buddha goes into a furnace. It comes out as coins. That scene, or one like it, belongs to a stretch of Chinese history when an emperor of the Tang dynasty turned on the monasteries. A Japanese monk named Ennin happened to be traveling in China then, and he kept a diary. In it he wrote about monks and nuns sent back to lay life, temples emptied, images taken away, and foreign monks like himself ordered to leave. Yesterday the power that protected the sangha also used it. Today, the same kind of power turns against it.

Start with China. Under the Tang emperor Wuzong, the court ordered monasteries closed and their lands and metal taken, and monks and nuns were made to return to ordinary life. Accounts point to more than one reason: money, land, bronze, and court politics that favored other teachings. Ennin's diary is one of the eyewitness sources. Now Japan, much later. When a new government came to power and set out to separate Buddhist and Shinto institutions, which had been woven together for a long time, a movement rose in some regions under a harsh slogan, haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni. Temples were closed or torn down, images were burned or sold, and some monks were forced out of their robes. Neither story is told here to cast anyone as a villain. Each is told because it happened. And then the second half, which is today's line. It endured. In China, practice went on, in small temples, in homes, in the chanting of the Buddha's name, and later rulers allowed monasteries again. In Japan, temples were rebuilt and communities regathered. The Buddha's last words, in the discourse on his final passing, already pointed at this. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buildings are component things. Bronze is. Estates are. What came through the furnace was people, still practicing.

Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: honor what endured. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something in your own life, or your family's, that came through a hard time. A recipe carried across a border. A prayer a grandparent kept saying when it wasn't safe. A friendship that survived a bad year. A habit you kept when everything else fell apart. Let it sit in front of you. Notice that the building, the job, the house, may be gone, and the thing itself is still here. Breathe with it, and let yourself honor it. The bell holds the time.
Persecutions. Times when rulers turned on monasteries, in Tang China and in Japan, and took the buildings, but not the practice. Today's word.
Your line: it endured. Today, when something you value gets knocked down, a plan, a routine, a hope, ask what part of it is still standing, and practice with that. Day one thousand thirty-three.

1034.title: Zen and war
1034.hook: some Japanese Buddhist institutions supported the war effort, and some later apologized
1034.howItsDone: Some Japanese Buddhist schools have issued formal statements of repentance for their wartime support, and Buddhist teachers today often point to the first precept and to this history when they speak about violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, persecutions: monasteries closed in Tang China, temples torn down in Japan, and the practice going on in homes. Your line: it endured. What part of your knocked-down thing was still standing? Day one thousand thirty-four.

A professional soldier, the head of a band of warriors, comes to the Buddha with a question. His teachers have told him that a warrior who dies fighting bravely goes to a heaven. What does the Buddha say? The Buddha tells him to drop it. Don't ask me that. The soldier asks again. Finally the Buddha answers, and it isn't what the soldier hoped. A mind set on killing in that moment, he says, leads to a bad rebirth, not a heavenly one. The soldier weeps. Not because he's been insulted, he says, but because he was deceived for so long. Keep that scene in mind. Today's story is about Buddhists who set it aside.

The first of the precepts that lay Buddhists take is to abstain from taking life. The Dhammapada puts the reason simply. In Max Muller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." Now the hard history. In the years leading up to and during the Second World War, some Japanese Buddhist institutions and teachers supported the war effort. Some Zen teachers wrote that the calm of Zen training and the soldier's readiness to die were the same thing, and that killing in the emperor's war could be selfless. Temples raised support for the war, and sermons blessed it. This was not every Buddhist in Japan, and some resisted and paid for it. But it was real, it was public, and it used the language of the practice. After the war, the reckoning came slowly. Then some Japanese Buddhist organizations, including Zen schools and Pure Land schools, issued formal statements of apology. They named their wartime support as wrong, and some said it betrayed the Buddha's teaching. That's today's line: apologies made. Why tell this in a lesson about practice? Because the soldier's question never goes away. Again and again, someone will say that violence for the right side is holy, and that a calm mind can do it cleanly. The Buddha's answer to the soldier, and the first precept, sit there in the texts as a check. And the apologies show a tradition reading its own scriptures again and saying, publicly, we got this wrong.

Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: sit with a hard truth. Let the body settle, and breathe. This time, turn toward your own record. Recall one thing you once defended, said or went along with that you now see differently. Something small is enough. Don't argue your case, and don't pile on blame either. Just let it be true, the way you'd let a heavy coat sit on your shoulders. Breathe in, knowing it. Breathe out, staying. If a wish to make it right comes up, let that be there too. The bell holds the time.
Zen and war. Some Japanese Buddhist institutions blessed a war that broke the first precept, and some later apologized publicly. Today's words.
Your line: apologies made. Today, if there's an apology you owe, even a small one, make it plainly, without explaining it away. Day one thousand thirty-four.

1035.title: Sri Lanka's war
1035.hook: in the long civil war, monks spoke both for war and for peace
1035.howItsDone: In Sri Lanka and elsewhere, Buddhist monks and lay groups hold peace walks, interfaith services and loving-kindness meditations for victims of violence on all sides, and Buddhists continue to debate the role of monks in politics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zen and war: a soldier weeping at the Buddha's answer, some teachers who blessed a war, and the apologies that came later. Your line: apologies made. Did you make one plainly? Day one thousand thirty-five.

Two clans stand on either side of a river, weapons out. The river is the Rohini, and the water is low, and each side says it needs the water for its fields. They are the Buddha's own relatives, on his father's side and his mother's. Tradition says the Buddha walks out between the two lines and asks a simple question. Which is worth more, the water or the blood of these men? There's no answer to that except to put the weapons down, and the story says they did. It's a story about the robe standing between armies. Today the robe stands on both sides of a real war.

Sri Lanka lived through a long civil war between the government and an armed separatist group, the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam. Civilians suffered on every side: Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Christian. Monks were part of that story in more than one way. Some monks spoke against peace talks and for a military victory, and some went into politics and campaigned on it. Some of them pointed to the island's old chronicle, the Mahavamsa. In one passage, after a war, a remorseful king is told by monks that the people he killed hardly counted, because they didn't follow the Buddha. Scholars and Buddhists argue about that passage, and many of them say it sits uneasily beside the first precept. Other monks walked a different road. They joined peace marches and interfaith gatherings, sat with families on the other side, and spoke against revenge after attacks. Lay Buddhist movements held peace meditations, people sitting together to wish for an end to the killing. And the Dhammapada has verses that tradition ties to the river quarrel itself. In Max Muller's translation: "Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!" So which monks were the real Buddhists? This path won't rank them. It tells you what each side said and which texts they reached for. The river story and its verse are there in the tradition. So is the chronicle. Today's line names the monks who reached for the river story and its verse: monks for peace.
screen: `SOME MONKS FOR WAR, CITING A CHRONICLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: pray for peace, or wish for it. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a place at war right now, or a place still healing from one. If you pray, you can pray for peace there, in words from your own tradition. If you don't, you can use the old wish from the discourse on loving-kindness: may all beings be happy, may they be safe. Let the wish include everyone in that place, both sides, the soldiers and the grandmothers. Then let it reach someone you yourself are in a small war with. The bell holds the time.
Sri Lanka's war. A long civil war in which some monks spoke for fighting and others marched, sat and spoke for peace. Today's words.
Your line: monks for peace. Today, in one argument, at home, at work or online, be the one who steps between the two lines and asks what's worth more. Day one thousand thirty-five.

1036.title: Myanmar
1036.hook: monks marched for their people; some monks have also spread hatred, and others have opposed them
1036.howItsDone: In Myanmar, giving food and gifts to monks is part of daily life for Buddhists, and the overturned bowl is a formal Vinaya act; monks and lay Buddhists there and abroad remain divided on nationalism, and some lead interfaith work for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sri Lanka's war: the Buddha between two clans at the river, and monks on both sides of a real war. Your line: monks for peace. Did you step between two lines anywhere? Day one thousand thirty-six.

Rows of monks in deep red robes walk through the streets of Yangon in the rain. They aren't shouting. Some are chanting the discourse on loving-kindness. And some are carrying their alms bowls upside down. To someone watching on the news, it looks like a protest sign. To people who know the monastic rules, it's something much older and very precise. An upturned bowl means: we will not accept your offerings. The monks were refusing gifts from the generals who ruled the country, at a time of hardship for ordinary people. In a country where giving to monks is part of daily life, that refusal was a loud thing to say without words.

The upturned bowl comes from the Vinaya. In the Cullavagga there's a case of a layman who falsely accuses a respected monk. The Buddha allows the sangha to turn the bowl down toward him: the monks won't visit his house or accept his food until he makes amends. It's a formal act, and it's meant to be reversed when the person changes. So when monks in Myanmar turned their bowls down to the generals, they were using an ancient rule as a kind of nonviolent strike. The marches were met with force; monks were beaten and arrested, and monasteries were raided. That is one face of the robe in modern Myanmar. Here is another, and it's hard. In the years since, some monks have preached against Muslims, including the Rohingya, spreading fear and hatred in sermons and online, while violence against Rohingya communities drove families from their homes. Those monks wore the same robe. And here is a third face. Other monks have spoken out against that hatred, sheltered Muslim neighbors during riots, and joined interfaith efforts, sometimes at real risk to themselves. The Dhammapada says, in Max Muller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good." This week ran from the last of the teachers into hard history. The teachers carried the lamp. Hard history, told because the community is made of people. Kings who protected and used. Persecutions endured. A war blessed, then apologized for. Monks for war and for peace. And now the same robe, used to refuse tyranny, used to spread hatred, used to shelter neighbors. Today's line holds on to the faces that refuse and shelter: the robe for peace.

Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: stand against one hateful word. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then remember the last time you heard someone speak with contempt about a group of people: a joke, a post, a comment at dinner. Maybe you said it. Don't punish yourself or them. Just hear it again, slowly, and notice what it does in the body. Then picture yourself answering it, calmly, with one sentence, the way a monk turns a bowl over: no shouting, just a clear refusal. Rehearse the sentence in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Myanmar. Where monks turned their bowls over to refuse the generals, where some monks spread hatred, and where others stood against it. Today's word.
Your line: the robe for peace. Today, if you hear one hateful word, about anyone, turn your bowl over: say your one calm sentence, and don't pass it on. Day one thousand thirty-six.
